host.note: 8 vCPU, 1 socket, 1 thread per core (no SMT), single NUMA node. Shared machine: other agents ran cargo/cc builds during parts of this session, so the final dataset was collected in windows where measured CPU busy was low and load average was ~1.8-2.8, monitored before and after each section.

sections.title: Process startup
sections.method: fork/exec wall time from spawn to process exit, median of 100 samples per runtime, all three runtimes interleaved within each sample and execution order reversed every repetition; stdout and stderr to /dev/null.

rows.note: Node and rustnode evaluate an empty program. Bun treats an empty `-e` argument as 'no command' and prints 2301 bytes of help text, so this Bun figure times help output, not an empty run; use the `void 0` row for a like-for-like Bun number.
Added as an equivalent empty-program control: `bun -e ''` prints its help banner instead of running an empty script.

sections.title: Peak resident memory
sections.method: peak RSS from wait4(ru_maxrss) over the lifetime of the process, maximum of 5 interleaved runs; the workload case requires fs, path, http and crypto and performs real work with each (read, hash, HMAC, RSA keygen, sign/verify, loopback HTTP).

sections.title: HTTP throughput
sections.method: identical hello-world http.createServer script per runtime; load generated by 6 separate Node 28 keep-alive client processes at concurrency 32 each for 4 s, median of 5 interleaved runs. A single client process saturates near 50k req/s on this host and would equalise all three runtimes, so six are used to make the server the bottleneck.

rows.case: hello-world, keep-alive, 6 clients x 32 concurrency, 4 s

sections.title: HTTP server memory under load
sections.method: peak RSS (VmHWM) of the server process measured immediately after a 4 s keep-alive load run at 6x32 concurrency, maximum of 5 runs.

sections.title: Native call overhead (process.cwd)
sections.method: 200,000 process.cwd() calls with a length check, self-timed with hrtime inside each runtime, median of 20 interleaved runs.

sections.title: Node benchmark tree
sections.method: each file invoked directly with one configuration (never run.js), median of 5 interleaved runs. Compare within a row only: different files, configurations and run counts are not comparable.

sections.title: Compatibility coverage
sections.method: Node's own test files, one process per file, scored with the four-marker rule from tools/test-tail-map.py: a file passes only when it exits 0, has no cross mark for a failing assertion, no Uncaught, no ‘1..0 # Skipped’ at column zero, and no ‘: # SKIP’. Exit-code-only counting inflates this suite by roughly 800 skipped files and must never be quoted.
sections.headlineNote: 3115 of 5714 Node test files across all eight suites, under the four-marker rule. This is a prior measurement at commits 1d020c12→293ae04c and was not re-measured in the three-way run. The 70.0% tile is a different and narrower figure — a this-session slice of test/parallel's first 300 files, which is a biased sample because Node's alphabetical ordering front-loads abort/assert/async_hooks. The two are not comparable and are not a trend. Bun's compatibility was not measured.

stats.label: test/parallel, first 300 files · this session at 365cfa2f

rows.note: Node is 100% by definition — these are Node's own tests. Bun's compatibility with Node's test suite was not measured: not because Bun is bad at it, but because Bun does not claim Node test-suite parity and the harness drives rustnode specifically, so the number would not be comparable to these.

null_control_js_loop.note: 20M integer adds, 10 warm-up passes before the timed pass. Should be 1.00x between Node and rustnode because rustnode reuses V8 unmodified: fast-path medians are identical (6.35 ms each, 1.00x). The plain medians differ because Node's first optimized pass loses a tier-up race in 13 of 30 runs (~83 ms), which rustnode never does (0 of 30). Bun runs the loop at 6.07 ms.
